column19: Fails Gate 1 (REJECT). Brookfield Corporation is a highly complex, multi-layered global conglomerate holding company whose economic risks and underlying asset values cannot be independently verified from the outside. While its 73%-owned asset manager (BAM) is an asset-light, transparent fee-collector, BN is the capital-heavy owner of equity residuals, unlisted private equity assets, commercial real estate (Brookfield Property Group), and expanding insurance/annuity liabilities (Brookfield Wealth Solutions). Internal mark-to-model Level 3 IFRS fair value accounting, complex unconsolidated affiliate webs, related-party capital recycling, and massive look-through leverage create structural opacity that violates the Munger circle of competence and verifiability standard. Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.
column20: Brookfield Corporation operates a labyrinthine corporate structure spanning dozens of public and private entities, including listed partnerships (BIP, BEP, BBU), direct real estate holdings (privatized BPY), and an expanding insurance balance sheet ($100B+ AUM across Brookfield Wealth Solutions / AEL). Key economic risks are invisible or unverifiable from reported figures: (1) Level 3 mark-to-model IFRS fair value accounting for vast commercial real estate (office/retail) and private equity portfolios, where minor 25-50 bps shifts in subjective capitalization and discount rates swing equity book value by billions; (2) Heavy consolidated leverage with >$200B in debt; while categorized as asset-level non-recourse, holdco cash flows are structurally subordinated to subsidiary debt covenants, and holdco capital is routinely deployed to backstop or inject equity into stressed affiliates; (3) Rapid expansion into fixed annuity reinsurance backing liabilities with internally originated alternative credit, introducing opaque long-tail actuarial and credit risks; and (4) Pervasive related-party transactions, management fees, incentive distributions, and asset transfers between holdco, listed affiliates, and private funds. This opacity directly contrasts with standalone BAM Ltd. (BAM.CA) and triggers an automatic structural rejection under Gate 1 standard (b).

Despite ~85%+ fee-based EBITDA and steady cash generation, capital returns are diluted by heavy fixed asset requirements. GAAP ROIC was 13.3% in FY22 (energy spike), then normalized to 8.4% in FY23, 6.8% in FY24, and 7.6% in FY25, yielding an 8.0% 5-year median.

column19: Rejected at Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing Power). Cameco is a premier nuclear fuel franchise, but remains a cyclical commodity producer. Earnings fluctuate wildly with spot potash and nitrogen prices. 5-year normalized GAAP ROIC (~8-9%) fails the 12% hurdle. Major structural threat from BHP's US$14B+ Jansen mega-project adding 8.5 Mtpa (~10% of global supply).
column19: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). The company has no ability to raise prices above inflation independently of global commodity supply/demand. Impending commercial startup of BHP's low-cost Jansen mine (Stage 1 in 2027, Stage 2 in 2031 adding 8.5 Mtpa) poses a structural supply shock.

Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.

Gold is an unconsumable store-of-value/monetary asset rather than an everyday Western functional necessity or ritual. Upstream mining requires massive capital reinvestment (sustaining & growth capex), with multi-year returns on capital (ROIC) fluctuating wildly between 3% and 10% across the metal cycle, failing compounder thresholds. Substantial production comes from jurisdictions with high political and regulatory risk, including Mali, DRC, Zambia, and Pakistan.

column10: Speculative commodity price-taker (gold mining) lacking essential Western utility; exposed to global commodity spot price cycles.

Heavy capital intensity (sustaining capex, mill expansions, tailings management) consumes a substantial portion of operating cash flow, precluding compounder-grade economic returns.

Downstream gates bypassed per waterfall.

column13: Unmatched global roll-to-roll converting scale across >200 plants in 40+ countries provides insurmountable procurement scale in resins, paper, and adhesives, combined with critical supply chain redundancy for global CPG and healthcare multinationals. column19: Passes all 6 gates. Global market leader in specialty pressure-sensitive labels, RFID inventory tracking, and surface-engineered barrier films. Structurally insulated across all 5 macrotrends; RFID inventory adoption and circular recyclable films act as secular drivers. column20: 5Y median GAAP ROIC of 13.1% and Tangible Operating ROIC of 30.8% reflect exceptional capital efficiency. column13: Physically unreplicable 20,000-mile contiguous right-of-way connecting Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf coasts forms an unassailable duopoly with CPKC. column20: 5Y median GAAP ROIC of 14.5% and tangible operating ROIC of 14.6%. Net debt of 19,950M CAD is ~4.2y owner earnings with strong 7.9x interest coverage and well-laddered long-term maturities, qualifying under the physical infrastructure solvency standard. Disciplined capital allocation with 28 consecutive years of dividend increases and steady share buybacks.

column13: Physically unreplicable 20,000-mile contiguous right-of-way forming the only single-line freight rail network connecting Canada, the United States, and Mexico. column19: Passes all 6 gates. The only single-line tri-national transcontinental freight rail network in North America (Atlantic to Pacific to Gulf of Mexico). Passes Gate 6 under the essential infrastructure standard with 82.0% FCF conversion, 7.3x EBIT interest coverage on long-dated debt, and active organic deleveraging from ~4.8y Owner Earnings following the transformational KCS combination. column20: Operates ~20,000 route miles linking major ports in Canada, the US, and Mexico (including Lazaro Cardenas, Saint John, Vancouver, and the US Gulf Coast). column13: Irreplaceable network of ~100+ permitted landfills and exclusive secondary-market municipal franchises creates localized disposal monopolies protected by insurmountable NIMBY zoning and EPA/provincial permitting barriers. column19: Passes all 6 gates under the v6.23 qualitative framework. Monopolistic North American solid waste and secondary-market landfill operator with industry-leading EBITDA margins (~31-32%) and 134% FCF conversion. Structurally insulated from all 5 macrotrends with renewable natural gas (RNG) acting as an energy transition tailwind. column20: 18.5% Operating ROIC (tangible return on capital unburdened by Progressive Waste merger goodwill) and 133.8% FCF/NI conversion. Core price yield consistently compounds at 6-9% annually with negligible churn. Owns/operates ~100+ permitted landfills across non-urban secondary markets in North America where alternative disposal options do not exist within economic trucking distances. Non-hazardous municipal waste collection backed by long-term exclusive contracts (5-10+ years) formulaically indexed to inflation.

column20: Canada's largest food and pharmacy retailer with over 2,400 stores (Loblaws, Superstore, No Frills, Shoppers Drug Mart). Reported FY2025 sales of $63.9B CAD, EBIT of $4.45B CAD, and Net Income of $2.67B CAD with median GAAP ROIC of ~16.1% and high FCF conversion. However, grocery retailing is a commoditized, high-volume, low-margin business where customer loyalty is low and price sensitivity is extreme. Sustained public hostility, parliamentary scrutiny, and competition from low-cost non-union operators (Costco, Walmart) structurally limit long-term pricing power.

column13: Regional grocery and pharmacy chain in Quebec and Ontario (Metro, Super C, Jean Coutu). While holding strong regional market share in Quebec, its 5-year median GAAP ROIC of 11.6% fails the 12.0% capital efficiency hurdle. Furthermore, it lacks unconstrained pricing power above inflation, constrained by aggressive price competition from national peers (Loblaw, Walmart, Costco) and regulatory scrutiny over grocery prices. Primary erosion threats: discount banner market share loss, warehouse club expansion, and pharmacy distribution cost pressures.
column19: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT). Disciplined regional food and pharmacy retailer in Quebec and Ontario, but fails Munger quality standards. 5-year median GAAP ROIC is 11.58%, strictly failing the >=12.0% proof-of-moat hurdle. In addition, Metro lacks independent pricing power above inflation due to intense price competition from Walmart, Costco, and Loblaw, combined with regional geographic saturation in Eastern Canada. Downstream gates nullified per strict waterfall.
column20: Operates ~950 grocery stores (Metro, Super C, Food Basics) and ~650 drugstores (Jean Coutu, Brunet). FY2025 revenue of $22.0B CAD, EBIT of $1.48B CAD, and Net Income of $1.02B CAD. Historical GAAP ROIC has persistently hovered between 10.6% and 12.4% (FY2022: 10.63%, FY2023: 12.38%, FY2024: 11.25%, FY2025: 11.91%; 4-year median 11.58%), failing the 12% cycle hurdle. Operating in a mature, commoditized supermarket industry with limited reinvestment runway outside Quebec and Ontario.

column13: Holding company controlling Loblaw Companies (~52%) and Choice Properties REIT (~62%). George Weston has no independent operational moat or pricing power of its own; its cash flows are entirely dependent on Loblaw retail dividends and Choice Properties rental distributions. Because its core underlying operating engine (Loblaw retail grocery) lacks unconstrained pricing power above inflation and faces intense political and competitive margin pressure, Weston fails look-through Gate 3b.
column19: Fails Gate 3b (REJECT). Holding company controlling Loblaw Companies and Choice Properties REIT lacks independent operational pricing power and fails the look-through moat standard. Underlying grocery retail operations at Loblaw are subject to intense political scrutiny, consumer boycotts, and price competition from Walmart and Costco that constrain pricing power above inflation. (Furthermore, consolidated leverage of >10x Net Debt/NI and sub-5x interest coverage would also fail Gate 6). Downstream gates nullified per strict waterfall.
column20: Holding company with primary assets consisting of a 52.6% controlling interest in Loblaw Companies Limited and a 61.7% controlling interest in Choice Properties REIT. Consolidated FY2025 revenue of $64.5B CAD, EBIT of $4.75B CAD, and Net Income of $1.10B CAD. Peak Owner EPS has collapsed from $5.33 CAD in FY2022 to $2.84 CAD in FY2025. Consolidated balance sheet carries $12.7B CAD in debt against $1.45B CAD in cash, yielding Net Debt to Net Income of 10.2x and EBIT interest coverage of only 4.15x.

column13: Saputo possesses significant dairy processing and distribution scale in Canada, the US, and internationally, but its product portfolio (fluid milk, cheese blocks, dairy ingredients) is heavily commoditized. It faces strong countervailing buyer power from national grocery chains and intense competition from private-label alternatives. Realized selling prices fluctuate with volatile dairy benchmark spreads (e.g. US block/barrel cheese) rather than independent pricing power.
column19: Rejected at Gate 3 (Moat & Pricing Power). Saputo operates in a structurally low-margin, commoditized dairy processing sector with severe private-label competition and no unilateral pricing power. Multi-cycle ROIC of 4-7% consistently fails the 12% economic moat hurdle.
column20: Operating margins have hovered tightly between 4.0% and 6.0% over FY2020-FY2025. 5-year median ROIC sits at ~5.2%, well below the cost of capital and the 12% Munger moat threshold. Substantial capital deployed on international acquisitions (Murray Goulburn in Australia, Dairy Crest in the UK) has failed to generate economic profits, proving the lack of structural pricing power.

column13: Direct overseas sourcing scale and unmatched Canadian store network density (>1,600 stores) yield the lowest retail cost structure in Canada. Successful rollout of multi-price tiers up to $5.00 demonstrated strong pricing power with zero customer churn, preserving 44-45% gross margins and driving GAAP ROIC >45% (Operating ROIC >80%). Primary erosion threats: wage inflation, supply chain disruption, and long-term domestic store saturation.
column19: Passes all 6 gates. Dominant Canadian extreme-value retail monopoly operating a classic scale economies shared flywheel. Unrivaled store density, overseas direct sourcing scale, <2-year store payback economics, and disciplined international compounding via Dollarcity (LatAm) and The Reject Shop (Australia). Pristine cash conversion (>110% FCF/NI) and interest coverage (>9.6x EBIT, >11.5x EBITDA) confirm negative equity was an accounting artifact of treasury share cancellations, not balance sheet distress. [5-10Y g: Canadian store traffic 2.0% + store network expansion (Canada, LatAm & Australia) 3.5% + multi-price tiering 1.5% + net share repurchases 2.5%]
column20: Operating ROIC >50% (GAAP ROIC ~22-26% including IFRS 16 lease liabilities, and ~45-57% on net operating assets). Free cash flow conversion averaged 115% of Net Income over FY2023-FY2026. Gross margins pristine at 44.7% and EBIT margins expanded to 27.1%. Net funded debt is $1.90B CAD against TTM Net Income of $1.31B CAD (1.45x Net Debt/NI, well below 4.0x ceiling) with EBIT interest coverage of 9.6x and EBITDA interest coverage of 11.9x. Uninterrupted peak-to-peak diluted EPS compounding from $1.78 in FY2020 to $5.39 in FY2025.

column13: Global fast-food franchisor with iconic brand intangibles (Tim Hortons, Burger King, Popeyes, Firehouse Subs) across 31,000+ units. The ~98% franchised model captures menu price inflation directly via percentage-of-sales royalties. Tangible operating ROIC exceeds 50%, though GAAP ROIC is ~9-11% due to $17.5B in acquisition goodwill. Primary erosion threats: franchisee margin squeeze from labor/food costs, market share losses to McDonald's, and aggressive discounting.
column19: Fails Gate 6 (REJECT). While Restaurant Brands International operates an asset-light, highly cash-generative fast-food franchise model (>100% FCF conversion) with entrenched everyday consumer habits (Tim Hortons morning coffee ritual, Burger King value dining), it structurally fails the Munger peace-of-mind fortress balance sheet standard. Legacy debt from 3G Capital's debt-financed acquisitions leaves QSR burdened with $15.7B in total debt and $14.5B in net debt against $776M-$1,021M of GAAP net income (14.3x to 18.7x Net Debt/NI, far exceeding the <=4.0x ceiling; 10.0x Net Debt/FCF). EBIT interest coverage is persistently depressed at 3.4x to 4.2x (4-year median ~3.86x), failing the >5.0x through-the-cycle requirement. With annual dividends ($1.1B) consuming ~75% of FCF, the company cannot organically retire debt and remains perpetually reliant on debt market refinancing ('kindness of strangers').
column20: Asset-light global restaurant franchisor (~98% franchised across 31,000+ units in 100+ countries). Free cash flow conversion is strong at >100% of GAAP Net Income ($1.45B FCF vs $776M Net Income in FY2025; $1.30B FCF vs $1.02B Net Income in FY2024) with low maintenance capex ($200-265M on $8.4-9.4B revenue). Tangible Operating ROIC is >50%, but reported GAAP ROIC is mediocre at 8.8% to 11.3% (5Y median ~9.7%) due to $17.5B in capitalized acquisition goodwill and brand intangibles. Structural Gate 6 failure is absolute: Total debt is $15.70B, Net debt is $14.54B, and Stockholders' Equity is $3.63B against negative tangible equity (-$13.86B). Net Debt to Net Income stands at 18.7x in FY2025 (14.3x in FY2024; 11.2x in FY2023; 13.2x in FY2022) and Net Debt to FCF is 10.0x, massively violating the 4.0-year Owner Earnings ceiling. EBIT interest coverage has failed the 5.0x threshold in every year of the cycle (FY2022: 3.67x, FY2023: 3.44x, FY2024: 4.06x, FY2025: 4.23x; 4-year median 3.86x). Dividends of $1.1B annually consume almost all free cash flow, leaving zero organic capacity for debt amortization.

column10: Wholesale printwear blanks and promotional apparel are discretionary corporate marketing and event purchases easily deferred during economic downturns.
column19: Fails Gate 2 (promotional apparel and wholesale printwear blanks are discretionary, deferrable corporate marketing and event expenses lacking Lindy consumer pricing power).
column20: Gildan derives the vast majority of its revenue from wholesale undecorated blanks sold into the screenprint, promotional merchandise, and corporate event channel. These purchases represent discretionary marketing and event expenditures that are rapidly curtailed during economic slowdowns. The business lacks consumer pricing power, is exposed to commodity cotton volatility, and recently suffered major governance instability ($76.8M proxy fight in 2024 resulting in complete board replacement).

column10: Broadline general retail (sporting goods, seasonal merchandise, housewares) and consumer credit card financing are cyclical, deferrable discretionary spending categories.
column19: Fails Gate 2 (general merchandise, sporting goods, and consumer credit card operations represent cyclical, deferrable discretionary spending rather than essential Western needs or Lindy consumer staples).
column20: Canadian Tire's primary retail banners (Canadian Tire, SportChek, Mark's, Party City) focus on discretionary merchandise categories such as sporting equipment, seasonal patio/outdoor items, and home decor, which are deferrable during economic downturns. Furthermore, its Financial Services division (Triangle Mastercard) introduces cyclical unsecured consumer credit risk. The company lacks secular pricing power against national and global retail competitors (Walmart, Amazon, Costco).

column13: Historical ROIC of ~8% falls below the 12% hurdle; thin operating margins (3-4% GAAP) and aggressive OEM buyer power eliminate structural pricing power above inflation.
column19: Fails Gate 3b (ROIC ~8% vs 12% hurdle; razor-thin margins of 3-4% and intense OEM buyer power leave Magna with zero structural pricing power).
column20: Magna's multi-year ROIC averages ~8%, persistently trailing its cost of capital and failing the 12% hurdle. Operating margins remain compressed at 3-4% GAAP (5-6% adjusted EBIT). Automotive OEMs possess immense countervailing power and enforce mandatory annual contractual cost downs, requiring Magna to negotiate commercial recoveries rather than exercising genuine independent pricing power.

column13: Mission-critical vertical market software deeply embedded in niche customer operational workflows with immense switching costs and low annual churn (<5%). Demonstrated pricing power via routine contractual 3-5%+ CPI-plus maintenance price increases.
column19: Passes all 6 gates. Elite decentralized acquirer and operator of mission-critical vertical market software (VMS). Ultra-high switching costs and customer workflow lock-in yield <5% gross churn and consistent 3-4% annual pricing power. Highly insulated from macro trends; AI coding aids internal developer productivity without impairing entrenched niche customer relationships. Self-funding acquisition engine with pristine balance sheet (net debt <1x FCF). [5-10Y g: organic volume 0.0% + price 3.5% + M&A reinvestment 7.5% - large-deal hurdle drag 0.5% + buybacks 0.0%]
column20: Operating ROIC >30% on tangible capital; 5-year median GAAP ROIC ~21.7%. Multi-year Owner FCF conversion exceeds 300% of GAAP Net Income due to heavy non-cash intangible amortization under IFRS and negative working capital dynamics (advance customer maintenance billings). Balance sheet is fortress-quality with $3.09B cash against $4.00B total debt (net debt ~$909M, or ~0.6x FCF). Mark Leonard's radical decentralization, zero-option compensation policy, and open-market insider buying mandate represent world-class capital allocation alignment.

column13: Multi-year government and enterprise IT outsourcing contracts provide baseline switching costs, but CGI faces intense competitive RFP bidding, client rate-card pressure, and limited pricing power unable to consistently outpace tech wage inflation. Primary erosion threats: commoditization of IT implementation and GenAI automated code generation compressing billable hours.
column19: Fails Gate 3b (Rejected – G3 Moat & Pricing). While CGI possesses switching costs in long-term government and financial IT outsourcing, it lacks structural pricing power above inflation due to competitive RFP rebidding, client rate-card pressure, and exposure to GenAI-driven coding automation compressing billable labor hours.
column20: CGI generates stable ~15-18% GAAP ROIC and >100% FCF conversion via disciplined M&A and outsourcing integration. However, as an IT services provider operating largely on fixed-price and billable-hour contracts, gross margins (~31%) have limited expansion capability against tech wage inflation. IT consulting is structurally exposed to cognitive automation (coding agents) reducing project person-hours, precluding pricing power above inflation.
